title_en: Zhejiang Textile Company v. Taiwan Li Rong Company — dispute over delivery of goods without original bills of lading under a contract of carriage of goods by sea
ruling_gist_en: 1. A shipper as defined in Article 42, paragraph 3 of the Maritime Code may be either the contracting party of a maritime cargo transport contract or the person who delivers the goods. A bill of lading is only evidence of the existence of a maritime cargo transport contract, and not the sole evidence. Where the party to the bill of lading is inconsistent with the party to the maritime cargo transport contract, and there is no written contract, the People's Court may determine the shipper under the maritime cargo transport contract based on the actual circumstances of performance of obligations.

full_text_en:
Zhejiang Textile Company v. Taiwan Li Rong Shipping Co., Ltd. — dispute over delivery of goods without original bills of lading under a contract of carriage of goods by sea

[Ruling Summary]

I. The shipper as defined in Article 42(3) of the Maritime Law may be either the party who concludes the contract of carriage of goods by sea or the person who delivers the goods. A bill of lading is evidence of the existence of a contract of carriage of goods by sea, but it is not the only evidence. When the party named on the bill of lading is inconsistent with the party to the contract of carriage of goods by sea, and in the absence of a written contract, the people's court may determine the shipper under the contract of carriage of goods by sea based on the actual circumstances of performance of obligations.

II. Where the shipper is unable to recover payment for the goods due to delivery without the original bill of lading, the carrier shall be liable to the shipper for compensation. When the shipper holds the original bill of lading that has not been transferred in trade and sues the carrier at the port of loading, there is no third party in the relationship under the contract of carriage of goods by sea who can claim delivery of the goods against the carrier by presenting the bill of lading, and thus there is no need to resolve the issue of whether the holder of the bill of lading has the right to take delivery of the goods.

Plaintiff: Zhejiang Province Textiles Import and Export Group Corporation, domiciled at: Zhonghe Middle Road, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province.
Legal Representative: He Zhiliang, General Manager of the company.

Defendant: Li Rong Shipping Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Minsheng East Road, Taipei City, Taiwan Province.
Legal Representative: Luo Yaohuang, Chairman of the company.

The plaintiff, Zhejiang Province Textiles Import and Export Group Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Zhejiang Textile Company), filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai Maritime Court against the defendant, Li Rong Shipping Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Taiwan Li Rong Company), regarding a dispute over delivery of goods without original bills of lading under a contract of carriage of goods by sea.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The plaintiff alleges that it has not yet received payment for the 21 batches of student uniforms carried by the defendant. Upon investigation, the defendant delivered these goods to others without presenting the original bills of lading. The plaintiff is both the owner of these goods and the actual shipper of these goods. Only based on trade arrangements did the plaintiff not list itself as the shipper on the bills of lading. The bills of lading issued by the defendant to the plaintiff were sent abroad by the plaintiff through collection; however, as no one redeemed the documents, they were returned by the bank. Consequently, the plaintiff is now the legitimate and lawful holder of these bills of lading and is entitled, in its capacity as shipper, to claim against the defendant for losses caused by delivery without original bills of lading. The plaintiff prays for a judgment ordering the defendant to compensate the plaintiff for: loss of payment for the goods in the amount of USD 2,602,562; loss of tax refund in the amount of RMB 3,111,486.35 (unless otherwise specified, all monetary units below are in RMB); discount interest loss in the amount of RMB 78,076.86; interest loss in the amount of RMB 2,555,234.67; attorney's fees in the amount of RMB 600,000; and attorney's travel expenses in the amount of RMB 20,000.

The plaintiff submitted the following evidence:
1. Two facsimile copies of Sales Confirmations, four originals of Letters of Credit, and a facsimile dated August 2001 from the foreign buyer, Company K, to prove that Zhejiang Textile Company was the exporter of the goods in question and the trade terms and prices for the goods;
2. Eleven domestic purchase and sale contracts, payment vouchers, special VAT invoices, special tax payment receipts for exported goods, tax refund documents, tax refund receipts, discount interest documents, interest calculation formulas, etc., to prove that Zhejiang Textile Company acquired ownership of the goods in question by entering into contracts and paying the purchase price to domestic manufacturers, as well as the domestic purchase prices, tax rates, refundable tax amounts, tax refund amounts, discount interest, and interest;
3. Foreign sales invoices, foreign exchange verification forms, freight forwarder certificates, freight invoices, and payment vouchers, to prove the quantity of the goods, foreign sales prices, transportation details, and payment of freight;
4. Manufacturer certificates, fleet certificates, packing lists from Taiwan Li Rong Company, declarations, courier receipts, vessel age certificates, and quality inspection certificates, to prove that the goods were shipped in accordance with the L/C requirements and delivered to Taiwan Li Rong Company for carriage;
5. Twenty-one sets of original bills of lading for the goods, to prove that the goods comprised 121,400 sets of student uniforms, with a foreign sales price of USD 2,602,562 and a domestic tax-inclusive purchase price of RMB 21,414,348.25; and further to prove that Zhejiang Textile Company is the holder of these original bills of lading;
6. Telex messages and correspondence from foreign banks, and a return document and explanatory letter from the Hangzhou Branch of the Bank of Communications, to prove that the 21 sets of original bills of lading were returned by the foreign bank due to non-redemption, and that Zhejiang Textile Company's current possession of these bills is legitimate and lawful;
7. Attorney's fee and travel expense receipts, to prove the corresponding expenses paid by Zhejiang Textile Company for the litigation.

Defendant's Defense: The defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company, argues: There is no concept of "actual shipper" in the law, nor has such a determination been made in judicial practice. Whether a person is a shipper must be determined by the记载 on the bill of lading. The defendant does not deny that the plaintiff once had ownership of the goods; however, after the bills of lading were issued, since the plaintiff was not named as the shipper on the bills, the plaintiff no longer has ownership of the goods. Therefore, the plaintiff cannot bring this lawsuit against the defendant in the capacity of shipper. The consignee named on the bills of lading in question is "to the order of the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research of Iraq" (hereinafter referred to as the Iraqi MoHESR). The reverse sides of the bills of lading currently held by the plaintiff bear no endorsement to order, therefore the plaintiff's possession of the bills is not lawful. The defendant has evidence proving that the goods under the bills of lading have been delivered to the Iraqi MoHESR as per the order on the bills. The defendant has fulfilled its obligations as carrier under the bills of lading in question, and regardless of who holds the bills, it should not be held liable for wrongful delivery of goods. The plaintiff's failure to receive the relevant payment was caused by its own recklessness or negligence in the trade contract. This is a dispute between the plaintiff and others under the trade contract, unrelated to the defendant, and the plaintiff's claims should be dismissed.

The defendant submitted the following evidence:
1. Booking notes, freight invoices, a description of the process of booking and shipping the goods issued by the freight forwarder Shanghai Samsun International Freight Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Samsun Freight) to Taiwan Li Rong Company, facsimile correspondence between Samsun Freight and Taiwan Li Rong Company concerning amendments to the contents of the bills of lading, and four booking notes and bills of lading for other goods shipped by Zhejiang Textile Company during the same period, to prove that there was no contact whatsoever between Zhejiang Textile Company and Taiwan Li Rong Company during the shipping and documentation process for the goods, that Zhejiang Textile Company was not the shipper on the bills, and that once Zhejiang Textile Company gave up its identity as shipper, its rights and obligations under the bills should also be relinquished, thus it has no standing to claim against Taiwan Li Rong Company as shipper;
2. A notarized and authenticated receipt from the Iraqi MoHESR for the goods, to prove that Taiwan Li Rong Company has fully performed its transportation obligations for the goods;
3. A legal opinion, to prove that certain legal scholars believe that, from a legal perspective, Zhejiang Textile Company cannot claim damages from Taiwan Li Rong Company on the grounds of delivery without original bills of lading.

The court presided over the examination of evidence and authentication. Following the examination of evidence, the Shanghai Maritime Court found the following facts:

On July 31, 2000, and August 7, 2000, respectively, the plaintiff, Zhejiang Textile Company, and the third party, Company K, entered into Sales Confirmations for 200,000 sets each of male and female student uniforms by facsimile. Subsequently, as the transferee and beneficiary of the irrevocable transferable letters of credit relating to this trade, it received documents under four letters of credit issued by the third party, HBZ FINANCE LIMITED. The documents under the letters of credit stipulated that the shipper was "ALHOSAN FOR IMPORT AND EXPORT / ALFARIS FOR IMPORT," the consignee was "to the order of the Iraqi MoHESR," and labels on the goods should display "ALHOSAN," "ALFARIS," or "FAST" in accordance with the buyer's arrangements.

Pursuant to the Sales Confirmations, the plaintiff, Zhejiang Textile Company, purchased the various types of garments in question from nine domestic manufacturers, including Dongyang Fashion No. 3 Factory Co., Ltd., by entering into purchase and sale contracts and making full payment of the domestic tax-inclusive purchase price. After the expiration of the shipment deadline and the validity period of the letters of credit, Zhejiang Textile Company nonetheless booked space and shipped the goods through a chain of agents at the port of loading: third party Huahai International Freight Co., Ltd. — Honghai International Shipping Freight Company — Shanghai Outerlink International Freight Co., Ltd., and Samsun Freight, in 21 batches for carriage by the defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company. The goods shipped comprised 86,900 sets of male student uniforms and 34,500 sets of female student uniforms. The total foreign sales price for these goods was USD 2,602,562, and the total domestic tax-inclusive purchase price was RMB 21,414,348.25. In compliance with the L/C requirements, Zhejiang Textile Company performed the procedures for issuing declarations, vessel age certificates, quality inspection certificates, etc. for the shipped goods and paid the ocean freight. Through the aforementioned freight forwarding agents, it obtained 21 sets of original negotiable bills of lading issued by the agent of Taiwan Li Rong Company, Shanghai United International Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. The consignee on these bills of lading was uniformly "to the order of the Iraqi MoHESR." At trial, Taiwan Li Rong Company confirmed that it had collected the relevant ocean freight. After the goods were shipped, the plaintiff, Zhejiang Textile Company, presented the full set of trade documents to HBZ FINANCE LIMITED through the Hangzhou Branch of the Bank of Communications for collection. As no one redeemed the documents, the full set of trade documents was ultimately returned by the bank to Zhejiang Textile Company. There was no endorsement to order of the Iraqi MoHESR on the reverse sides of the returned documents. At trial, the defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company, confirmed that it had transported the goods in question to Iraq and delivered them to the Iraqi government-designated Iraq State Shipping Company, which then delivered all goods to the Iraqi MoHESR. Accordingly, none of the original negotiable bills of lading for the goods were retrieved.

Issues in Dispute: (1) Whether a person whose name does not appear in the "shipper" column of the bill of lading has standing to bring this lawsuit as shipper? (2) Whether Taiwan Li Rong Company is liable for delivery without original bills of lading? (3) How should the economic losses caused by delivery without original bills of lading be determined?

The Shanghai Maritime Court held as follows:

The relevant clauses on the reverse side of the bills of lading stipulate that any dispute or claim arising from the bill of lading shall be subject to the court and law chosen by the carrier (the defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company). Such court and law may be the court and law of the carrier's principal place of business, or the place of loading or delivery, or the port of shipment or discharge. After the Shanghai Maritime Court confirmed its jurisdiction over this case, both parties, and particularly Taiwan Li Rong Company, explicitly expressed their willingness to choose the Maritime Law and the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter Contract Law) to resolve the dispute. Out of respect for this choice, the Maritime Law and the Contract Law are determined as the applicable law to define the rights and obligations of the disputing parties.

Regarding the First Issue: The Hamburg Rules, adopted at the United Nations Conference on the Carriage of Goods by Sea held in Hamburg, Germany, in March 1978, for the first time defined a shipper in the carriage of goods by sea as: a person who concludes a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier (hereinafter "contracting party") or a person who actually delivers the goods to the carrier (hereinafter "delivering party"). With reference to this definition, Article 42(3) of the Maritime Law provides: "'Shipper' means: 1. a person who, by himself or through another person acting in his name or on his behalf, concludes a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier; 2. a person who, by himself or through another person acting in his name or on his behalf, delivers the goods to the carrier in connection with the contract of carriage of goods by sea." From a grammatical and textual interpretation, the Hamburg Rules separate the contracting party and the delivering party with the word "or," thus the shipper under the Hamburg Rules can only be one of these two types of persons. In contrast, the Maritime Law lists the contracting party and the delivering party side by side, separated by a semicolon, thereby indicating that both the contracting party and the delivering party can be considered "shippers" under the Maritime Law. Since the Maritime Law does not mandatorily require that the delivering party, when acting as shipper, must be named on the bill of lading, whether a delivering party can be a shipper is not legally conditional upon its name appearing on the bill. Article 72 of the Maritime Law provides: "After the goods have been received by the carrier or loaded on board, the carrier shall, upon request of the shipper, issue a bill of lading. The bill of lading may be signed by a person authorized by the carrier. A bill of lading signed by the master of the ship carrying the goods is deemed to have been signed on behalf of the carrier." Based on the established facts, the plaintiff, Zhejiang Textile Company, after completing the purchase from various domestic manufacturers, through each link of the freight forwarding agents, booked space with the defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company, paid freight, and delivered the goods for shipment. Taiwan Li Rong Company, likewise through each link of the freight forwarding agents, accepted the goods, collected the freight, and issued the bills of lading as requested by Zhejiang Textile Company. Apart from Zhejiang Textile Company, there is currently no evidence that any other person delivered the goods to Taiwan Li Rong Company and instructed it on how to perform the contract of carriage of goods by sea. Although Zhejiang Textile Company did not have its name stated on the bills of lading due to trade arrangements, the aforementioned facts prove beyond doubt that it was the contracting party and the sole delivering party under the contract of carriage of goods by sea. Under normal circumstances, the transfer of ownership of goods requires the payment of consideration. There is no evidence in this case that Zhejiang Textile Company transferred ownership of the goods to any other person. Taiwan Li Rong Company's claim that Zhejiang Textile Company transferred its ownership of the goods merely because it was not named as the shipper on the bills of lading lacks sufficient factual and legal basis. If the bills of lading had been validly transferred in trade, they should have borne an endorsement to the order of the Iraqi MoHESR. A prerequisite for such an endorsement is that the MoHESR had lawfully held the bills. Zhejiang Textile Company adduced evidence proving that the bills were returned by the bank due to non-redemption after collection. The Iraqi MoHESR never saw the bills and thus could not have endorsed them. Given that the bills of lading have not entered valid trade circulation, Zhejiang Textile Company holds bills returned by the bank due to the failure of the trade, which is equivalent to holding the bills in the capacity of the cargo owner or the first holder after issuance. Thus, its possession of the bills is legitimate and lawful, and it is entitled to assert corresponding rights under the bills against the opposing party. In fact, in the more than two years since the goods were shipped, no person other than Zhejiang Textile Company has presented the original negotiable bills of lading to Taiwan Li Rong Company to claim corresponding rights under the bills. Taiwan Li Rong Company has, by its own conduct, implicitly recognized that Zhejiang Textile Company is the contracting party and the sole delivering party under the contract of carriage of goods by sea. Otherwise, it would have had no reason to prepare the bills as requested by Zhejiang Textile Company and its freight forwarders, and even less reason to have the bills it issued circulated through the freight forwarding agents to Zhejiang Textile Company, making it the first lawful holder of the bills after issuance. Accordingly, it shall be determined that Zhejiang Textile Company has standing to bring this lawsuit as the shipper of the goods.

Regarding the Second Issue: Article 71 of the Maritime Law provides: "A bill of lading is a document which serves as evidence of the contract of carriage of goods by sea and the receipt of the goods by the carrier, and as a guarantee by the carrier to deliver the goods against it. A clause in the bill of lading stating that the goods shall be delivered to a named person, or to order, or to bearer constitutes a guarantee by the carrier to deliver the goods accordingly." Article 79 provides: "The transfer of a bill of lading shall be carried out according to the following provisions: (1) A straight bill of lading shall not be transferred; (2) An order bill of lading shall be transferred by endorsement, either special or blank; (3) A bearer bill of lading may be transferred without endorsement." Article 107 of the Contract Law provides: "If a party fails to perform its contractual obligations, or performs them in a manner inconsistent with the agreement, it shall bear liability for breach of contract by continuing performance, taking remedial measures, or compensating for losses." A bill of lading is a guaranty document issued by the carrier. Delivering goods covered by a bill of lading only against presentation of the original bill is a duty the carrier guarantees to perform. This has long been a well-established maritime custom. This custom requires the carrier to deliver the goods under the bill to the holder of the bill of lading (who, in normal trade, is the person who has paid, or at least ostensibly promised to pay, the trade consideration). It plays a vital role in maintaining normal trading order and has thus been adopted by legislators. After all, carriage of goods by sea serves trade. Although the defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company, attempted to prove that it delivered the goods under the bills to the Iraqi MoHESR in accordance with the order on the bills, it had to admit that it did not retrieve the original negotiable bills of lading when delivering the goods. As a carrier, performing its obligations in such a manner does not comply with the contract of carriage of goods by sea, nor does it conform to maritime custom and legal provisions. Therefore, it is liable for breach of contract and shall compensate Zhejiang Textile Company for the actual losses suffered as a result of the delivery without original bills of lading. The cause of action in this case is a dispute over delivery without original bills of lading under a contract of carriage of goods by sea. Unless Taiwan Li Rong Company can prove with sufficient evidence that its delivery without original bills was caused by Zhejiang Textile Company's fault in the trade, thereby exempting it from liability, the issue of whether, or to what extent, Zhejiang Textile Company was at fault in the trade falls outside the scope of this trial. Taiwan Li Rong Company's argument that "the plaintiff's failure to receive the relevant payment was caused by its own recklessness or negligence in the trade contract, that this is a dispute between the plaintiff and others under the trade contract unrelated to the defendant, and that the plaintiff's claims should be dismissed" is not accepted.

Regarding the Third Issue: Article 55(1) of the Maritime Law provides: "The amount of compensation for loss of goods shall be calculated based on the actual value of the goods; the amount of compensation for damage to goods shall be calculated based on the difference between the actual value of the goods before and after the damage, or the cost of repair." Article 113(1) of the Contract Law provides: "If a party fails to perform its contractual obligations, or performs them in a manner inconsistent with the agreement, thereby causing losses to the other party, the amount of compensation for losses shall be equal to the losses caused by the breach, including the benefits that could have been obtained after the performance of the contract, but shall not exceed the losses that the breaching party foresaw or ought to have foreseen at the time of concluding the contract as possibly resulting from the breach." The defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company, breached the contract at the port of destination by delivering the goods under the bills to others without retrieving the original bills, thereby separating the documents and the goods. Although the plaintiff, Zhejiang Textile Company, now lawfully holds the full set of original bills of lading for the goods, it is unable to transfer the bills to deliver the goods to others and thereby recover payment for the goods. Taiwan Li Rong Company shall be liable to compensate Zhejiang Textile Company for the losses thus suffered. The existing evidence shows that the losses suffered by Zhejiang Textile Company include: the foreign sales price of the goods in the amount of USD 2,602,562, which is the payment Zhejiang Textile Company would have received under normal trade conditions and also the actual value of the goods; the tax refund amount of RMB 3,111,486.35, which is the sum Zhejiang Textile Company would have received under normal trade conditions in accordance with the relevant provisions of the state authorities; and interest calculated on the two sums — USD 2,602,562 from the normal foreign exchange receipt date of January 2001 to the end of September 2002, and RMB 3,111,486.35 from the state-stipulated tax refund date of July 2001 to the end of September 2002 — at the enterprise demand deposit rate. This interest represents the legal fruits Zhejiang Textile Company would have received under normal trade conditions and constitutes part of its actual losses. The above sums shall all be compensated by Taiwan Li Rong Company.

The plaintiff, Zhejiang Textile Company's claims against the defendant, Taiwan Li Rong Company, for discount interest loss and corresponding interest on the discount interest loss were calculated based on local policies formulated by the Zhejiang Provincial Government to encourage export earnings. Local policies are effective only within a specific administrative region and do not have universal binding force externally; therefore, this claim of the plaintiff is not supported.

Although the legal fees and travel expenses for lawyers for which Plaintiff Zhejiang Textile Company sought compensation from Defendant Taiwan Li Rong Company were expenses incurred by Zhejiang Textile Company in support of the litigation, since there are no clear provisions in existing laws and regulations on this part of the claim, and also because there is currently no unified, specific, and practically operable calculation standard for this part of the claim, it is currently difficult to support it.

Accordingly, the Shanghai Maritime Court, on December 25, 2002, by Civil Judgment (2001) Hu Hai Fa Shang Chu Zi No. 441, rendered the following judgment:

1. Defendant Taiwan Li Rong Company shall, within 10 days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate Plaintiff Zhejiang Textile Company for the loss of货款 (proceeds of goods) in the amount of USD 2,602,562, and the bank interest calculated on that amount from January 1, 2001, to September 30, 2002, at the current enterprise demand deposit interest rate of the People's Bank of China;

2. Defendant Taiwan Li Rong Company shall, within 10 days from the effective date of this judgment, compensate Plaintiff Zhejiang Textile Company for the loss of tax refund in the amount of RMB 3,111,486.35, and the bank interest calculated on that amount from July 1, 2001, to September 30, 2002, at the current enterprise demand deposit interest rate of the People's Bank of China;

3. The other claims of Plaintiff Zhejiang Textile Company are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 149,541.02 shall be borne by Plaintiff Zhejiang Textile Company in the amount of RMB 17,030.95, and by Defendant Taiwan Li Rong Company in the amount of RMB 132,510.07.

On November 28, 2002, Li Rong Shipping Company merged with Taiwan Evergreen International Storage and Transportation Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Evergreen Storage Company). After the judgment of first instance, Evergreen Storage Company, dissatisfied with the judgment, appealed as the successor of the rights and obligations of Li Rong Shipping Company, on the following grounds: 1. The shipper as defined in Article 42, paragraph 3, item 2 of the Maritime Code must be the person himself or a person who entrusts another to act in his own name. The first instance judgment found that the appellee entered into a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the appellant through other entities, but these "other entities" did not enter into the contract in the name of the appellee, so that the appellee was not recorded as the shipper in the bill of lading. This is sufficient to prove that there was no contract of carriage of goods by sea between the appellee and the appellant. 2. Although the appellee formally and "legally" held the bill of lading, it could not take delivery of the goods at the port of destination because it had not obtained instructions from the I-Kao Department of Education, and therefore was not a holder of the bill of lading within the meaning of the Maritime Code, and could not have rights and obligations under the bill of lading legal relationship with the appellant. 3. A bill of lading is not a document of title; a person entitled to take delivery of the goods does not necessarily have obtained ownership of the goods. The issue of ownership of goods can only be confirmed in the trade contract, which is not within the scope of this case. The shipper recorded in the bill of lading is not the appellee, and it cannot be proven that the appellee is the owner of the goods under the bill of lading. Where the ownership of the goods has not yet been determined, the appellee, by filing a lawsuit merely on the basis of a bill of lading that cannot be used to take delivery of goods, has unclear rights that it seeks the legal protection of. 4. Ordering the appellant to compensate the appellee for the loss of tax refund is without legal basis. It requested the second instance to amend the judgment.

The Shanghai High People's Court, upon trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Shanghai High People's Court held that:

A bill of lading is only evidence of a contract of carriage of goods by sea, and not the sole evidence; a bill of lading cannot be equated with a contract of carriage of goods by sea. Article 42, paragraph (3), item 1 of the Maritime Code provides that a shipper means a person who, himself or through another acting in his name or on his behalf, enters into a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier. Article 73 provides that the absence of items such as the name of the shipper in the bill of lading does not affect the nature of the bill of lading. It can be seen that the law does not require the shipper to enter into a contract of carriage of goods by sea with the carrier personally; the shipper may entrust another to enter into the contract with the carrier. The law permits the shipper to request the carrier not to record the shipper when issuing the bill of lading, or to record another person as the nominal shipper; the shipper's doing so does not affect the nature of the bill of lading. This is because the shipper is exercising his own rights, and the consequences arising therefrom are borne by the shipper. This request does not increase the carrier's responsibilities; the carrier is still only responsible for the carriage and delivering the goods to the consignee designated by the shipper, so there is no need to refuse it. The subject recorded in the bill of lading may only be the formal party to the contract of carriage of goods by sea; in practice, situations where the subject of the bill of lading is inconsistent with the subject of the contract of carriage of goods by sea do exist. In the absence of a written contract, the parties to the contract of carriage of goods by sea can be determined based on the actual circumstances of the parties' performance of obligations, and cannot depend entirely on the records in the bill of lading.

In this case, although there were several layers of agencies acting as intermediaries, it was only the appellee, Zhejiang Textile Company, that delivered the goods to the appellant, Evergreen Storage Company, paid the freight, and made specific requests for the preparation of the bill of lading; the other companies were all performing agency work. Evergreen Storage Company, completely in accordance with Zhejiang Textile Company's request, recorded three foreign companies as the nominal shippers when issuing the bill of lading, delivered the bill of lading to the freight forwarding company entrusted by Zhejiang Textile Company, and collected the freight paid by Zhejiang Textile Company from the freight forwarding company. This fact is sufficient to prove that it was Zhejiang Textile Company and Evergreen Storage Company that established a de facto contract of carriage of goods by sea. The first instance finding that Zhejiang Textile Company was the contracting party of the contract of carriage of goods by sea and the shipper of the goods under the bill of lading in question was not improper. Evergreen Storage Company's ground of appeal that there was no contract of carriage of goods by sea between the two parties lacks factual basis and legal support and is not adopted.

The appellee, Zhejiang Textile Company, in its capacity as shipper, holding the original bill of lading at the port of shipment, sued the appellant, Evergreen Storage Company, as the carrier for breach of contract by delivering goods without the original bill of lading, causing it the loss of being unable to recover the货款 (proceeds of goods), and claimed damages. As a party to the contract of carriage of goods by sea, where the carrier, Evergreen Storage Company, delivered goods without the original bill of lading, the shipper, Zhejiang Textile Company, certainly has the right to request the carrier to compensate for the loss of being unable to recover the proceeds of goods caused by the delivery without the original bill of lading. If this right of the shipper were denied, it would be equivalent to making the shipper, who performed its obligations in accordance with the contract, bear the consequences of the carrier's breach, which is clearly inconsistent with the principle of fairness, contrary to legal provisions, and detrimental to maintaining social and economic order. Where the bill of lading in question is held by the shipper at the port of shipment and has not been transferred in trade, there is no third party who can claim the right to take delivery of goods from the carrier based on the bill of lading in the contract of carriage of goods by sea relationship, so there is no need to resolve the issue of whether the holder of the bill of lading has the right to take delivery of goods. Evergreen Storage Company's grounds of appeal that Zhejiang Textile Company is not a holder of the bill of lading and has no right to take delivery of goods are of no practical significance to Zhejiang Textile Company's holding of the bill of lading and are not directly related to the handling of this case, and are not adopted.

In this case, the appellant, Evergreen Storage Company, delivered goods without the original bill of lading, causing the appellee, Zhejiang Textile Company, not only to be unable to recover the货款 (proceeds of goods), but also to suffer a loss of tax refund due to its inability to meet the conditions for export tax refund. These losses were foreseeable and should have been foreseen by Evergreen Storage Company when it committed the breach of contract by delivering goods without the original bill of lading. The first instance judgment ordering Evergreen Storage Company to compensate for these losses is consistent with the provisions of Article 113 of the Contract Law of the PRC.

In summary, the facts found in the first instance are clear, the law applied is correct, and the judgment should be affirmed. The grounds of appeal of the appellant, Evergreen Storage Company, are all unsustainable and should be dismissed. Accordingly, the Shanghai High People's Court, in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) and Article 158 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, on September 4, 2003, by Civil Judgment (2003) Hu Gao Min Si (Hai) Zhong Zi No. 39, rendered the following judgment:

Appeal dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed.

After the final judgment, Zhejiang Textile Company applied to the Taoyuan District Court of Taiwan for recognition of the civil judgments of the Shanghai High People's Court and the Shanghai Maritime Court. On August 11, 2004, the Taoyuan District Court of Taiwan, by Civil Ruling (Sheng Zi) No. 1032, ruled to recognize the civil judgment (2003) Hu Gao Min Si (Hai) Zhong Zi No. 39 of the Shanghai High People's Court and the civil judgment (2001) Hu Hai Fa Shang Chu Zi No. 441 of the Shanghai Maritime Court. Evergreen Shipping Company filed an objection and a further objection with the Taiwan High Court and the Taiwan Supreme Court, both of which were dismissed.
